title: A resident who is not herself

bedside.infusions: Baseline checked: {not isNull(chartAt)|yesno}. RN told: {not isNull(reportAt)|yesno}.

banner.text: The RN supervisor is at the bedside.

objective: Recognizing the client whose condition requires immediate RN or provider involvement
secondaryObjectives: Give a clear handoff, using a structured tool such as SBAR -- situation, background, assessment, recommendation -- when reporting a concern

Contribute to the six clinical judgment steps -- recognize and analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes -- within the PN role, reporting findings that need RN or provider judgment
What the practical nurse license permits, and where it stops

sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 (primary PDF): Coordinated Care 18-24% of items, including 'Provide care within the legal scope of practice'; Physiological Adaptation: 'Recognize and report change in client condition'; Reduction of Risk Potential: 'Monitor and evaluate client vital signs'. The test plan does not name SBAR.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles (the PN collects data and reports findings that need RN or provider judgment; SBAR as a structured handoff tool).

brief.situation: 14:00 in a long-term care home. You are the LPN for one hall; the RN supervisor covers the building. A nursing assistant stops you: Mrs. Alvarez in Room 22, 82, 'isn't herself today'. She didn't eat lunch and is very sleepy.
handover: Mrs. Alvarez has moderate dementia and lives here long term. The assistant says she usually walks to lunch with her walker and chats.
Standing orders allow the LPN to take vital signs, SpO2 and a fingerstick glucose, give oxygen at 2 L by nasal cannula for SpO2 below 92%, and encourage fluids.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Collect the data you need, compare it with her baseline, and decide who needs to know. Some steps take a few minutes.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at 16:00, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Untreated, her infection progresses to septic collapse about 1 h 40 min after 14:00. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Once the provider's plan is under way, she slowly stabilizes. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Severity at which she becomes unresponsive and hypotensive. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Vital signs and SpO2: about 3 min.
RN supervisor to the room: about 10 min.
RN reaches the provider and gets orders: about 15 min.
Authored: the RN told within 15 min of the first abnormal vital signs.

cues.question: What cues tell you this is a change that needs the RN now, what might be causing it, and what is your part as the LPN?

parts.label: Cues and the likely cause
parts.criteria: Names an acute change from her baseline (new drowsiness and confusion, not eating, fever, HR and RR up, BP down from her usual) rather than 'her dementia'; ranks infection (likely urinary, from the dark foul urine and low intake) as most likely and serious, and notes glucose has been ruled out.
parts.modelAnswer: This is an acute change, not her dementia: she is usually chatty and walking, and now she is drowsy and confused, not eating, febrile, tachycardic and tachypneic, with a BP well below her usual. Dark, foul urine and very little intake point to a urinary infection, possibly sepsis. Her glucose is normal.

parts.label: The LPN's part
parts.criteria: Collects data (vital signs, SpO2, glucose, urine and intake, comparison with baseline), gives only standing-order care, reports at once to the RN with an SBAR that names the change and asks the RN to come and contact the provider, documents objectively; does not sedate her, give unordered drugs, or wait.
parts.modelAnswer: Collect the data and compare it with her baseline, use the standing orders (fluids, oxygen if SpO2 is below 92%), and report now to the RN with an SBAR: an acute change, likely infection, please come and assess and call the provider. Document objectively. No sedation, no leftover antibiotics, no waiting until the end of the shift.

noProgress.rationale: A resident with an acute change still unreported to anyone who can act at 16:00 is deteriorating unattended, so this case calls it harm.

kpis.label: Abnormal vital signs to an effective report

expertPath.text: Go and look: drowsy, confused, dry. Vital signs and SpO2, a fingerstick glucose.
Check the care plan: her baseline is chatty and walking, BP 130s/70s. Yesterday's dark urine; 300 mL in today. Fever, HR and RR up, BP down: an acute change.
SBAR to the RN: acute change, likely infection, please come and assess and call the provider. Offer fluids; oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%.
RN at the bedside; provider orders a transfer. Objective note; update the daughter.

collapse.headline: She collapsed on the hall
collapse.body: The assistant's 'not herself' was the first cue. Find when vital signs were taken, whether they were compared with her baseline, and when the RN heard it as an acute change.

transferred.headline: Recognized, reported, transferred
transferred.body: You collected the data, compared it with her baseline, reported an acute change with an SBAR that asked for what she needed, and stayed within your scope. That is the expert path.

transferredLate.headline: Transferred, by a slower route
transferredLate.body: She is on her way, but check how long the report took, whether it sounded routine, whether you checked her baseline, and whether anything outside your scope was given.

time_up.headline: Nobody who could act saw her
time_up.body: An acute change in a resident with dementia is reported, not explained away. When the first answer is to wait and she keeps worsening, report again.

scoring.modelReasoning: 'Not herself' from a nursing assistant is a cue to act. The LPN collects data (vital signs, SpO2, glucose, urine and intake) and compares it with the resident's baseline from the care plan: new drowsiness and confusion, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea and a pressure well below her usual mean an acute change, most likely an infection (urinary here), possibly sepsis, not her dementia. Report it at once to the RN with an SBAR that names the change and asks the RN to come and contact the provider; give only standing-order care; document objectively. Sedating her or giving unordered drugs is outside the LPN's scope and hides or worsens the problem; waiting to recheck later lets her deteriorate.

baseline.ask: While you take her vital signs: what will tell you whether these numbers are a change?

choices.label: Her own baseline in the care plan

baseline.explain: Her baseline. In long-term care a BP of 108 can be a big drop for someone who usually runs in the 130s; compare with her own record, then report the difference.

scopeQ.ask: While the RN comes: which of these is within your role right now?

choices.label: Recheck her vital signs and stay with her
Tell the daughter she has a UTI

scopeQ.explain: Collect and report data and stay with her. Starting an unordered drug is outside the LPN's scope, and naming a diagnosis to the family is not the LPN's to make.
